title: Rabbah's joke: the Talmud laughs
hookLine: puns, jokes and absurd cases fill its pages
carry: a joke first, then learning in awe

cards: Before the lesson, a joke. Tractate Shabbat says that the sage Rabbah, before he began teaching, would say something funny, and his students would laugh. Then he would sit in awe and begin.
A joke first, then the work. It's a small detail, and it says something about the book it sits in. A text this serious has room for laughing, and sometimes the laughter is part of the teaching.

teach.b: The Talmud laughs in more than one way. There's wordplay.
The prophet Isaiah promises that all your children will be taught of the Lord, and great will be their peace. The Hebrew for your children is banayikh.
A teaching at the end of tractate Berakhot says: don't read it banayikh, your children. Read it bonayikh, your builders. The ones who learn become the builders of peace.
One small change in sound, and the verse opens. Then there are the absurd cases, pushed to the edge to see where a rule breaks.
The Mishnah says a young bird found within fifty cubits of a dovecote belongs to the dovecote's owner.

teach.h: ONE FOOT IN, ONE FOOT OUT.
teach.b: Rabbi Yirmiyah asked: and if one foot is within fifty cubits and one foot is outside? The Talmud reports, completely deadpan, that for this question they put him out of the study house.
Readers still differ about whether he was teasing or deadly serious, and whether the sages were annoyed or laughing too. And then there are the mice.
In tractate Pesachim, a house has been searched for leaven before Passover.
A mouse goes in with bread in its mouth. A mouse comes out with bread in its mouth. Same mouse?
The sages work it through with complete seriousness, and that's the comedy: great minds at full power, chasing a mouse. Why keep all this on the page? Partly because a sharp case sharpens a rule.
Partly, like Rabbah's joke, because a laughing mind is an open one. On these pages, seriousness and laughter sit at the same table.

how: In yeshivas and study partnerships, learners often enjoy the Talmud's wordplay and its strange hypothetical cases, and teachers sometimes open a class with something light before turning to the text.

o: mocking the rabbis' rulings as foolish and outdated
a folk custom of jokes told about well-known rabbis
jokes, puns and odd cases kept on the pages beside the law

games.q: who laughs where — tap the pairs.
p: began each lesson with a joke
one foot in, one foot out

s: the Talmud has no jokes or wordplay in it
it keeps puns, absurd cases and a teacher's opening joke on its pages.
Rabbi Yirmiyah asked about a bird with one foot on each side of the line
and the Talmud says they put him out of the study house for it.
the mouse with bread in its mouth appears in tractate Pesachim
a house searched for leaven, a mouse going in and a mouse coming out.

games.q: you're Rabbah, about to teach a room of tired students a hard lesson. how do you begin?
o: go straight into the hardest part.
say something funny, let them laugh, then begin in awe.
games.why: tractate Shabbat says he began with something funny, the students laughed, and then he sat in awe and taught.

practice: Bring back something that once made you laugh because it was clever: a pun, a riddle, a child's question that stumped the grownups. Let it be funny again, and notice where the smile starts. Then ask, lightly, what it taught you.

wordCard.voice: The Talmud laughs. Puns, absurd cases and a teacher's opening joke, kept on the same pages as the law, because a sharp case and an open mind both help learning. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: your builders, the reading Berakhot puts in place of banayikh, your children (Isaiah 54:13).

carryVoice: Your line: a joke first, then learning in awe. Rabbah made his students laugh before the lesson, and the Talmud keeps its puns beside its law. I'll be here tomorrow.
